query: Research on refractory multicomponent alloys has emphasized exceptional strength at room and elevated temperatures, while mechanical assessment has relied mainly on compression and has included relatively few tensile studies. WFeNiMo fragments released more chemical energy than tungsten-alloy fragments in thin-steel-target penetration tests, and HfZrTiTa0.53 was reported at 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain. This evidence establishes strength and energetic promise but leaves limited tensile ductility, load-bearing reliability, and processability unresolved. Subject to preserving strength and impact-triggered energy release, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention for HfZrTiTa0.53 that could improve tensile ductility and uniform elongation? Include the intervention, causal mechanism, directional or quantitative outcomes relative to the reported baseline, the applicable temperature, loading mode, and strain-rate limits, prior evidence from the cited studies, and matched compression, tension, and impact tests with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermomechanical treatment—specifically, applying a moderate cold reduction (≈8–10% strain) followed by a sub-transus anneal (around 950°C for 1 hour with controlled cooling)—will refine the microstructure of as-cast HfZrTiTa0.53, thereby enhancing its tensile ductility and uniform elongation while preserving its high strength and impact energy release characteristics.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTiTa0.53 produced by conventional casting with a coarse, possibly heterogeneous microstructure exhibiting a yield strength of ~786 MPa, compressive strength ~1314 MPa, and limited tensile ductility (terminal strain ~13.5%).
generation.intervention: Apply a thermomechanical treatment involving moderate cold rolling (≈8–10% reduction) followed by annealing at sub-transus temperatures (≈950°C for 1 hour) with controlled cooling to promote recrystallization.
generation.conditions: Testing at room temperature under quasi-static loading conditions (strain rate ~5×10−4 s−1) for tensile tests, with matched compression and impact tests to evaluate load-bearing and energy release performance.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention is expected to produce a refined and more uniform, equiaxed grain structure by inducing recrystallization and reducing internal residual stresses, which leads to a homogeneous distribution of microstructural features that facilitate uniform plastic deformation.
generation.mechanism: Cold reduction introduces a sufficient density of dislocations that, upon annealing, drive recrystallization to form fine and uniformly distributed grains. This refined microstructure reduces stress concentrations and delays the onset of localized necking under tensile loading, thereby improving ductility. Meanwhile, the overall phase composition and strength-bearing features remain largely intact, preserving high yield and compressive strengths as well as impact-triggered energy release.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in uniform tensile elongation from ~13.5% to roughly 20–27% while maintaining yield strength near or above 700 MPa and compressive strength around 1300 MPa, with no detrimental impact on the material’s energy release performance during impact tests.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 with reported tensile properties of 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected under room temperature, quasi-static tensile conditions (strain rate ~5×10−4 s−1); effects may differ at elevated temperatures or under high strain-rate impacts, where the recrystallized microstructure might exhibit different dynamic responses.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal annealing temperature and time window that maximizes ductility without lowering strength; additional trial processing may be needed to balance recrystallization with retention of strength and impact energy release. Moreover, scale-up and potential anisotropy following rolling require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfZrTiTa0.53 samples: one set processed with the proposed thermomechanical treatment (cold rolling at ≈8–10% reduction followed by annealing at ≈950°C for 1 hour with controlled cooling) and a control set in the as-cast condition. Conduct room temperature tensile tests (strain rate ~5×10−4 s−1), compression tests, and impact tests under identical conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the treated samples do not show a statistically significant increase in uniform tensile elongation (i.e., improvement less than ~20% increase relative to the 13.5% baseline) or if there is a significant degradation (>10% drop) in yield strength, compressive strength, or impact energy release compared to the as-cast samples.

With the decrease in temperature, the yield strength, tensile strength, and elongation after fracture increase simultaneously. The yield strength and tensile strength of the alloy at 77 K are 476 and 1211 MPa, respectively, and the elongation after fracture is 66.8%. Three variants of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) from the AlCoCuFeNi group, containing different amounts of Al and Cu, were developed and produced via induction melting and casting into ceramic moulds. The ingots were homogenized at 1000 °C for 10 h. Analyses revealed that variations in Al and Cu concentrations led to significant changes in the material’s microstructure, hardness, strength, and impact strength. In the equiatomic variant, differential scanning calorimetry revealed a peak associated with the phase transformation, indicating that this alloy’s microstructure consists of two distinct phases. In contrast, when the concentrations of Al and Cu are reduced, a single-phase microstructure is observed. The equiatomic variant (used as a reference) is characterized by its hardness and brittleness, exhibiting slight ductility, with a tensile strength of 80 MPa, a hardness of 400 HV5, and an impact strength of 1.9 J/cm2. However, with adjusted Al contents of 1/2 and Cu contents of 1/4, the alloy displays exceptional strength combined with good plasticity, achieving a tensile strength of up to 450 MPa with 60% elongation, and an impact strength of 215 J/cm2. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa.
